utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, Thomas Laugel, and Kathleen Childs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's Christopher Gosnell for Goran Hadzic along with Liane Aronchick our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. On Monday, the 1st of July, the Trial Chamber has been instructed not to sit due to the opening ceremony of the Residual Mechanism. I would have the parties to note that we will not sit on Monday, the 1st of July. Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just while that's taking place, a waiver was filed, I believe, yesterday for Mr. Hadzic's absence for the last session today. And -- and he would respectfully request permission to be absent for that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to not sitting on the 1st of July, is it be possible the Chamber might be amenable to sitting on Friday of that week which would not push us off schedule for the following week with the witness logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll discuss that during the first break, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McElligott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you comfortable where you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McElligott. Are you hearing me loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could I ask you again today to speak very clearly and slowly again because we're speaking the same language and to leave a pause after my questions. Thank you. Now, at the end of the day yesterday, you were describing measures that UNCIVPOL took to address crimes and you said that the people with responsibility for addressing the crimes, the 7.000, as you described them, could have made a significant impact on these communities. This is transcript 6023. What types of measures could the RSK police have taken to reduce or prevent crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary function of a policeman and of a police service is to prevent crime. And to do that, you have to be visibly active in your community, you have to be very much in contact with your community, and you've got to have respectability of your community. And I think they were deficient in many of those fields. It is clear that a minority group were afraid to report crimes to them, they didn't report crimes to them, and there is no doubt - only for the involvement of our monitors - many crimes would have gone unrecorded, not to mind being investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Final question. Your evidence that you've provided has various examples of the RSK police being involved in crimes against civilians. What impact did the police involvement in crimes have on the non-Serb inhabitants of these areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this instance, we're talking about the special police. I'd like to distinguish that there were what I would regard as two different fields of people. And one were the professional police officers, and many of them behaved in a very professional manner. There's no doubt about that and we have to acknowledge that to them. But on the other side of the house, there was a group and they did not function in a policing way. In fact, I would say they were the problem. And we have many instances where they are engaged in criminal activity, they have been reported by witnesses as seeing in militia uniform, and there are many accounts where they behaved improperly in the sense that we have reports where they would go into a community or a town and literally shoot up the place, discharge fire-arms, and that brought a reign of terror. I have accounts of my own monitors where this happened at night-time, and they would jump up from their beds and lie on the floor until things settled down again. And that was happening inside of small communities, and there's no doubt it had a terrible impact on people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes the questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gillett. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McElligott.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. McElligott, my name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I'm going to ask you a few questions today. If anything is unclear, please feel free to ask me to elaborate or clarify and I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And always remember, sir, please to observe a pause after the end of -- of my question and the start of your question [sic].

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I'll try my best as well not to -- to observe a pause after your answers. Now, before Mr. McElligott before we get into a discussion of the crimes that you observed and your reporting of those crimes in some of the documents indicating crimes, I'd like to talk about the context of your mission. And at paragraph 13 of the your statement, you say: "The role of the UN troops was to ensure that the area remained demilitarised and that all persons in them would be protected from fear and armed attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we could just please bring up L2, which is Defence tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Am I correct in characterising the overall concept of the Vance Plan to be that there would be a military element of UNPROFOR whose primary responsibility was to ensure protection for the United Nations Protected Areas and that there would be a police element, UNCIVPOL, that would monitor law enforcement within those protected areas? Is that a fair overview of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- yes, indeed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention there to paragraph 7. And let's, first of all, look at the language that seems to be the basis for what's in your --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apologies, I just have a difficulty with the distance on sight. So could it be enlarged a little. Could the size be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on paragraph 7. A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that all right, Mr. McElligott?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could enlarge a little more. My apologies. Yeah go ahead. Yeah, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, there, we see the -- the third sentence: "The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack." Now, that language is a little bit strange. It says "protecting them from fear" as opposed to protecting them from armed attack. Would you agree, though, that for everyone on the ground the understanding was to prevent those protected areas from coming under attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have to take a step back before we look at that and there was to be a demilitarisation before these things came into effect. So, in other words, the conflicting parties were to withdraw and demilitarise and then UNPROFOR took up its responsibility of managing a demilitarised area. And it's within that environment the local police would function as well. So, in reality, we were never there at that beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in an imperfect world, and UNPROFOR was certainly operating in an imperfect effect world, and we're going to look at some documents as we go along that address this, it was nevertheless - notwithstanding that there had been insufficient withdrawal by Croatian forces from the confrontation lines and insufficient or incomplete demilitarisation within the protected areas - nevertheless, it was UNPROFOR's goal and mandate to protect those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the initial commitment was given and undertaken by those signing up to the agreement, they had a role to fulfil. And they didn't do it. And we found ourselves in the middle of that conflict, trying to handle a brand new situation and an extremely difficult situation. So while we were there -- and negotiations were taking place from the one man on the ground level to, I'm sure, at UN headquarters level to try and bring people to a point where let's go back and start at the beginning and try and achieve what you set out to do and what you agreed to. In the meantime, we were functioning and running inside of that environment where there was total conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, two sentences forward, it says here in paragraph 7 of the Vance Plan: "As the United Nations Force assumed its responsibilities in the United Nations Protected Areas (UNPAs) all JNA forces deployed elsewhere in Croatia would be relocated outside the republic." Now looking at that formulation, would you agree with me that the bargain that appears to be reflected here is that the JNA is withdrawing in exchange for UNPROFOR coming and providing security for the UNPAS?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally there is a transition period where when the place becomes demilitarised and UNPROFOR establishes itself, and I think I have set out some dates there in relation to UNPROFOR establishing itself in Sectors North South, East and West. In reality, they were on the ground prior to those dates, but being established takes a certain period of time, and they declared it where they had taken responsibility even though they were in there perhaps months in advance. So you can see there was a leeway to get to the point where you could say, "I'm available and I'm ready now," and hopefully when they were declaring that, the other parties would have come to the position where they would leave them in a functional state. But that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me try to approach this from a different angle. Amongst your Serb interlocutors, did you understand that they were looking to UNPROFOR to provide protection, military protection, for the UNPAs from Croatian attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer it probably in this way in the sense that I've said it before. I'm there as a policeman with a particular role to play. There were political levels to be engaged in, there were military levels to be engaged in, and there I'm sure is plenty of evidence available as to what measures they took along the way on those issues, so I don't think I should go off into the politics of it or go into the military end of it. There is lots I'm sure who can account for those things. So I -- I can look at it from my policing point, and all I can say to you is: We were not where we expected to be when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You were in the region for how long?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 13 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how frequent were your contacts with Serb officials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Serb officials, I would say very -- very little with officials because the commissioners of the day went to the meetings and the only times I did attend specific meetings were in Geneva and Vienna, and, again, I would have been there perhaps as an observer in a sense to the negotiations and available in the event of issues arising in relation to policing matters or policing plans that may emerge from the negotiations so that would be my level of involvement, on the ground, with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our commissioner and both commissioners, actually, attended. But the political and civil affairs side of it was dealt with by civil affairs so they focused on what would be the political end of the mission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You were kept abreast of the content of the contacts that your bosses, namely the commissioner of UNCIVPOL, was having with the Serb side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were kept abreast of the contacts that the political affairs, civil affairs people, were having with the Serb side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would be reasonably familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And many of the documents -- and let me ask one more question on that line. You were kept abreast as well of contacts that some of the people on the military side, including the Force Commander, was having with the Serb side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would be aware of meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And many of the documents that you have been asked to authenticate and comment upon are indeed from the military side and the civilian affairs side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. So are you in a position to comment on contacts that the civilian affairs and military people were having with the Serb side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on the documentation I've seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have 1367, please, which is Defence tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have seen the court reporter's note on the screen, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am going to do my utmost. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a code cable, possibly, it's a communication, in any event, from General Nambiar to Mr. Goulding at the United Nations in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps this should not be broadcast. I'm not sure whether the Prosecution can assist me. It is on the Prosecution list, and I -- I don't recall what the standard policy is on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you just give me 30 seconds, I can check. I don't think there's a problem, but I'll just check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In the meantime, perhaps it's best not to broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can go over to page 2, please. And this is reflected also on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We see that this is a letter from the state committee for co-operation with UNPROFOR of the RSK government. Now, can I first ask you, Mr. McElligott, did you know that there was a state committee for co-operation with UNPROFOR in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a variety of committees. I would be familiar with the fact that there were numerous committees of linking and talking to each other, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the date of this letter is the 10th of November 1992, so are you in -- in country at this point; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged a little, please. Thank you. A little more. Oh. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And here we have Mr. Zecevic righting to Mr. Nambiar, General Nambiar, and I want to draw your attention to a couple of passages here. "It should be repeated that the basic reason for accepting the Vance Plan was a total security of the population in the protected territory provided by the presence of the UN troops, i.e., your task defined in Article 7 of the Vance Plan which we quote: 'The role of the UN troops would be to ensure that these areas remain demilitarised and that all the inhabitants in these areas be protected from the threat of armed attack [sic].'" "This provision of the Vance Plan was the main reason to accept it. In my deepest conviction, this provision expresses the very essence of the Vance Plan and this is why we insisted on it in all our contacts with the representatives of UNPROFOR." Now if we please go down the page: "But what is unacceptable for us is your attitude that the cease-fire is violated by the Croatian side because the total demilitarisation has not been carried out in the protected areas. Such a logic is completely unacceptable and absurd. "Likewise, we insisted on having your answer and guarantees for complete realisation of the obligation under point 7 of the Vance Plan, and no adequate response has been given, least of all a positive one." Now let me just start with the last point there. Were you informed or do you know whether UNPROFOR told the Serb side that they could not guarantee the territorial protection of the protected areas from Croat attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to the first point to perhaps address the issue and it is -- starts with a point that it would remain demilitarised, which would suggest that when UNPROFOR started, they were starting with a demilitarised situation, and going forward you can see how complex it was, how lacking in trust there was on both sides because you can see where the Croatian side failure or threat of coming towards the Serbian was an issue. And there's a total lack of trust being seen there, and that's where UNPROFOR found themselves with having to negotiate. And it -- they -- they start with remaining demilitarised which would suggest it should have taken place. But neither side had moved and one was saying, Well, if you move, I'll move, so it's -- where do we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they're setting out their position to say, "Look, we see a problem on the far side of the fence." I'm sure the other people were saying the same thing. And that's where UNPROFOR would have to sit in and try and bring them to that point again. So that's the complexity of it. That's the environment we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At this point, the JNA had withdrawn, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the area was not demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- I -- I -- as to who had withdrawn, I can't be specifically sure. The military would know who specifically had done what. So that can be obtained from them. I can't provided you with details on the military element of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just a quick note, we checked. There's not a problem with that document. It's been cleared to be used publicly. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I thank my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: In your time there, did you see where UNPROFOR forces were deployed? How were they dispersed in the UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had -- UNMOs were basically on the front line, as I understand it, on both sides as liaison officers. There was a battalion of military, UN military in a very - how do you call it? - sector. In fact, there may be a couple of battalions in some sectors so that they were dispersed throughout the region, throughout the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they in any way oriented towards the limits of the protected areas? In other words, were they stationed in such a way that they could, first of all, observe; and, secondly, protect or prevent incursions into the UNPAs from the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge of them is that they had a military base in all the areas, that the troops were there. And how they actually deployed, I don't know because we dealt with the policing side when we needed and indeed we had drawn on the reserves to help us. They were available to us, and we knew about that level of participation. And as for their absolute functions and how they performed, I won't account for that nor I do it -- can I do it. They were there and I have no doubt they were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reason I ask you and the reason I think you're in a unique position to comment on this is that you had, if I'm not mistaken, 600 CIVPOL monitors scattered in some cases into the far reaches, I would say, of the protected areas; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had monitors literally in every community right up to the -- right inside the pink zone. We had several stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your monitors and you, when you toured --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can I just ask you, how often did you yourself tour [Overlapping speakers]?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be of a random nature. Initially, I went for two weeks just to establish myself on the ground and know what was out there, and I went to every police station we had and met, I would say, most of our people. So when I got back I knew what I was looking at when people spoke to me. So I would -- apart from that, then I would have gone, I would say, quite often in a sense. You know, that if something happened that needed to be seen, and I talked about going down to Benkovac. I was in Medak pocket, I was in -- come to various other places, other sectors, so I would have a reasonable input into travelling around the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've just referred to pink zones. What were the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pink zones were -- they were established by way of an additional resolution to the UN Protected Areas. That there were areas outside the UNPAs and they were in Croatia, and they were up to the full confrontation line, and basically they were occupied by the JNA and were the dominant or -- not dominant, but the overall -- the majority population was Serbian. So their resolution then was that the UN mission could function there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there were CIVPOL monitors in the pink zones right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had several stations pink zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it was UNPROFOR's view, as with the protected areas, that there should be no military attack from the Croatian side on the pink zones, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. And if can I recall correctly, there was a -- the confrontation line, I think there was a 5 kilometre, let's say, no man's land between the two parties to create a vacuum or to divide, keep them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would a fair summary of the disposition of UNPROFOR forces be that their battalions to a very large extent were located centrally in some major centre in the sectors, and that they, in effect, sent out patrols towards the confrontation lines, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks were located in -- I suppose in the simple sense they -- they -- they were provided with barracks because of -- that's where the space was and the scope was to locate them. How they patrolled, that is what they do, and I suppose in a sense they were looking at their operational matters and patrolling in an effective way to meet that desire. We were doing it to meet our results, and I'm sure they can account for how they did it. But you can see from the military reports the activities they engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It is -- are we talking about the document 1367, the Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The witness hasn't confirmed any of the contents. He hasn't really adopted this document. In fact, he's said on a number of occasions that he couldn't offer comments on it. So we don't think the sufficient nexus has been established for this. We don't have a problem in terms of the format as it is attached to a document, but we don't think the witness has added any particular value and his evidence is clear enough on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That as may be, but I am surprised that the Prosecution - and this isn't the first time - is objecting to the admissibility of documents on its own exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I apologise for interjecting here, but on that point, we've got a 65 ter list in this case that consists of over 6.000 documents put together during a time of intense trial preparation. Yesterday, the Chamber declined to allow the Prosecution to add an exhibit to its list. The point being that simply because something's on the list doesn't mean that it's admissible by either side. And so the suggestion simply that it's on the list does not signify that it's admissible or that it is otherwise stands on its own. It's within the universe of potential exhibits. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained for failure of nexus with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McElligott, at paragraph 55 of your statement, and perhaps we could bring that up. This is 6363. It's now P2168. And I -- I suppose -- do you have it there in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Yes, Your Honours, I have it. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So at page 17 there's a heading entitled: "Incursions into the Sectors by All Sides to the Conflict." And it reads: "There were incursions over the UNPA demarcation lines by all parties to the conflict. The incursions by the Croatian side included operations in Benkovac in January 1993 and in Maslenica and the Medak pocket in September 1993." Now I note you say there were incursions by all sides but then the only examples you give are incursions by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is there a clarification that you would wish to make in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In that matter, I referred to "by all sides," and in doing that, I was also including the - what would you call it? - the -- the -- what do you call it? Explosions or attacks by military operations. Not just personal attacks by individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shelling -- sorry. Shelling is what I mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Violations of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... shelling, yeah. So I generalised it in that sense by both sides, but in this instance I'm referring to incursions of the type I am specifying here which would be on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But during the entire period of 1992 and 1993, isn't it true that the only side that crossed confrontation line with troops that that been established was Croatian forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have cited what I know here, and on recall, I would think - and I remember reading it again - there was one minor one at the front line, and I think it just got to the front line before again it was headed off in some fashion probably by negotiation and discussions, but it wouldn't have got into a serious situation. Not to the scale we're looking at here. It was of a minor nature, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me put the question again because I don't think I got a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's understandable, sir, I'm not criticising you. As far as you know, the only side that crossed the confrontation line that had been established at the time of the Vance Plan with troops were Croatian forces --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in 1992 and 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, that's my situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in addition to the examples you've cited, did you know there was an attack on a place called Miljevacki Plateau in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of it referred to and perhaps read something about it somewhere along the way. But, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were Croatian forces still in Miljevacki Plateau when you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I can't. I don't know. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D468, please, which is Defence tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a video which I believe and hope we should be able to broadcast. And can you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And let's -- let's just play it and then I'll ask you some comment, some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Where is Niper? What do you mean you didn't? I am left without everything. What are you talking about? Take him with us. The Croatian army in the hinterland of Sibenik completed a successful action of the liberation of Miljevac. We got these -- this footage later. "He has two golden teeth."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that footage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, my understanding is that this video was shot by Croatian forces. They took the video. And apparently in 1992, it was subsequently shown on television and it became somewhat infamous, certainly on the Serb -- amongst the Serb population in the protected areas, particular in Sector South as being one of the incidents that occurred during the Miljevacki Plateau operation. Did you ever hear any of your monitors or did you yourself hear from the Serb side that they were concerned about the manner in which Serbs had been abused during this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we referred to the report yesterday of the 27th of July where there was a substantial volume of crimes recorded in respect of Croats. I know that our monitors also interviewed numerous, indeed, I think all Serbian people who came from outside of the United Nations protected area on -- when they arrived and documented accounts from them. And, again, there are horrific accounts. You know, we have some terrible stuff in that report of 27th of July. I think you will find the same in the other one. And you can see the level of abuse. We saw an account yesterday from Kjel Johansen, where he met a man who had been beaten. He was in bed and in a terrible state. So the human brutality is visible. It's appalling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what kind of impact did this have, as far as you were able to learn, on the confidence of the Serb side in the UN's ability to protect either the pink zones or the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to look at it in this way is that both sides had endured the situation. UNPROFOR was coming in as a new pair of hands to try and start a new beginning and stop this and put -- start again and hopefully get people to see a new -- a new vision of where they wanted to go. And I think that's where UNPROFOR was coming from, is to get people to stand back, enter negotiations, I know it's going to be -- it won't happen in a week or it won't happen in ten years, I go back to my own country. Perhaps it took 15 years to get to an agreement. But we got there. And it's still been [inaudible]. So, you know, you are dealing with an appalling situation with a historical background and there is no simple answer. All you could hope is that the leaders would lead and that they would work in the direction of gaining peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But this occurs in June 1992, almost immediately after the arrival of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the first time that the entire structure or the bargain of the Vance Plan, so to speak, is tested, there's a failure in -- in -- and when I say "failure," I -- I don't know mean to impugn any one person. I mean to say that the objectives, the laudable objectives that you've just described, those objectives were not being fulfilled in this incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this environment, you're going to take one step forward and two steps back very frequently. And you know, that is the way you had to go. You're not going to have a magic wand and say, "Everything changes today." You are -- the change you are about to make is monstrous and all you can do is hope that UNPROFOR would get in there, give the guidance, give the leadership, and leadership would come from other places, and eventually over time that you can build -- you're looking at something. Not sorting a problem out today, you're looking at sorting out the future. And it has to be looked at in that scope. And the UN being there for six months is only getting your leg in the door. You could be there for 20 years and still working at it. So the change you have to make and indeed -- you can see how people would be terrorised on the ground. I mean, looking at it was frightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How did this incident in particular or more generally the events of Miljevacki Plateau affect based on what you were able to observe or learn intercommunal, interethnic tensions in Sector South and Sector North?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an amazing environment. On the ground in the community, before I suppose the troubles broke out there was a -- an interrelationship between communities in -- in a friendly sociable way, and we have had many monitors who have been approached in the sector when they were going on breaks outside of it to say, "My neighbour has been kicked out. When you go to wherever you're going, would you convey my greetings." They never fell out. Now, when you go to other levels, the levels of hatred came in, politics came in, and the dynamics changed. But on the ground with society, there was still a bond of friendship and a bond of good neighbourship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, could you look back on the screen to my question? And I -- I was just wondering if you could focus on that specific point.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The film is still in display.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please assist the witness with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's at line 21, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in difficulties with my eye-sight. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me just repeat it then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The question was how did this event and the other events that people knew about as having occurred at Miljevacki Plateau, how did that impact upon intercommunal tensions in Sector North and Sector South in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they have a very destabilising effect. You know, there's a -- people would not sleep in their bed at night when they know that there's a risk of attack from one corner or another. That -- that's -- it has a serious impact on the community, and again you're back to trust, mistrust. You know, there's total -- the place is just totally unstable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that impacted on the ability of both you and the police to maintain law and order in Sector South, in particular, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It made things extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No objection. We note there's no transcript in e-court for this. On a previous occasion where this has come up, I noted that it got MFI'd pending a translation being added. So I'd suggest if we follow that, that procedure, would be -- we'd have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the parties know now -- know more than we do, but do we have any elements to know what this video is, when it has been filmed, who the people are on the -- on -- on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, my -- I was only able to rely on open sources for this information, so I cannot vouch for its -- for the reliability of the information I have. I can only say that I have a good-faith basis to belive that it is what I described it to be in court, and if Your Honours are not comfortable with that, then we'll tender it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Unless I suppose parties agree on what it is and where it comes from and when it has been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No, we're not aware of that information. As I said, we haven't had a transcript in e-court either, so, yeah, we're in the dark, just as Your Honours are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: For the time being, Mr. President, we'll put this on the back burner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01273, please. Defence tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a crypto-cable from General Nambiar to Marrack Goulding. The date is the 22nd of September. The third sentence reads: "In these circumstances, you might perhaps feel able to impress upon Tudjman, as we sought to do yesterday with Milas in Zagreb, the imperative necessity of the Croatian army pulling well back from Peruca and behaving immaculately for a change." First of all, let me ask you: Do you know -- do you have any information that would help us understand why General Nambiar would use that particular expression, namely, that the Croatian army should behave immaculately for a change?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect that he grounding it on a previous profile of activities and that he is seeking a higher standard in how things are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in general did you observe provocative actions while you were there or did you learn about provocative actions by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, let me just finish my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Other than the specific incursions that we've already talked about and that you've mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I'm not familiar with any that I can recall right now. If there were activities, say, in the pink zones where our monitors would be close to the front line, they would be reported in our sitreps. But asking me that right now, I just can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you recall anything about this incident being referred to in Peruca?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect you're referring to the Peruca dam here, so that's what became a serious area of contention in the sense that from what I'm aware it was mined with perhaps the objective of blowing it and that would could caused major flooding and destruction of property and people. Everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Peruca in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that Croatian forces threatened frequently to seize the dam by force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was a contentious issue and that it was mined. As to the politics of it, I'm not too sure. But I was very aware of it, the risks of it. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Generally, did you learn from your monitors in their contacts with Serbian police that they were concerned about an incursion by Croatian forces in Peruca?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there was a situation there. It was -- let's put it, always a risk of heightening the tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I ask you, were police, regular police now, I'm talking amongst the 7.000, were those regular police liable to perform duties other than law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- at any time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the situation reports and accounts given by them for not being available or performing would indicate that they were being sent -- some were being sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the regular police could be sent to the front line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I know it has been presented as a reason for not being available. So I take it on face value that they may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In any event that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That account has been given to us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: By -- your own monitors reported that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our mon -- yes, it would -- it would be seen in situation reports that on occasions they called to a station and there was nobody -- I think there is one specific one there for Sector South where there was nobody available on a particular day, and I think the account given was everybody was on the front line or engaged. I think that could go around to the Maslenica bridge occasion. And I think I referred to it earlier, that we thought they would have at least left one person behind to honour the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So let me just understand this. You're saying that there was a situation when all or most or all of the regular police officers in a police station left that station, left their regular duties, and were sent to the front line to respond to whatever threat may have been occurring there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if they went there or what happened, but that was presented as the reason why they didn't engage on a particular day. And I made the point at the time as saying that they thought -- we thought somebody would be left behind or at least somebody would be available to deal with it. So I don't know where they went, but they certainly weren't available. One could take the view as well that in view of hostilities they were just going in another direction at that particular time. I don't know, and to be fair I don't want to nail it down one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your monitors were reporting that they were leaving --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- for that reason?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that a frequent occurrence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequent, I wouldn't refer to it as frequent, but I know it has appeared on occasions. I wouldn't consider it a frequent situation, and I think the circumstances of meetings and so forth wouldn't -- wouldn't justify that as being the case. There were police available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This document is tendered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D69, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1254, please, Prosecution tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that I believe is referred to in your report, although I don't have a paragraph reference, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could assist. It's paragraph 113 of the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there, at the -- that doesn't seem to be the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a status report on the Serbo-Croatian conflict and UNPROFOR mission. It's dated 7th of September, 1992. No authorship is indicated, but, sir, you -- you've probably looked at this document. Based on the idiom, the way in which it's written, can you tell us who you think wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you enlarge it a little, please. I would -- I would associate it with perhaps a civil affairs-type document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is this a document -- would it probably have been authored by Mr. Andreev?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, September 1992 ... I think -- yes, oh I can't say he authored, but I think Viktor was in the mission when I arrived. He was because we -- we met because -- we had met in Namibia, so I would have recalled him in the sense when I met him as meeting with somebody from the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was head of civil affairs in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 says: "UNPROFOR's mission is still in a military phase." And your statement echos that at one point. Can you tell us what that means, that UNPROFOR's mission was in a military phase?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think basically what he is say something that demilitarisation has not taken place, and they find themselves in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how does that impact on UNPROFOR's duties or role?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go back to the Vance Plan again. The basic concept of what your functions were couldn't be fulfilled because the pitch was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3, please. At the top of the page it reads: "Risks of military action to restore Croatian authority are indeed realistic. Croatian side's patience and good will is reaching the point of non-return. They seem to react out of pure nationalism. "October is a deadline for them and therefore a turning point for the whole operation. "Provocation/retaliation process is intensifying. Pressure on the front line from Croatians increases daily under form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians. Clashes and incidents between milicija and Croatian police are expanding daily. The confrontation might result from this milicija's like trend with probable intervention of CA followed by the opening up of heavy arms stores to back it. Mobilisation is probably ongoing overnight." Now, I just want to focus in particular on the part where he says "pressure on the front line from Croatians increases daily under form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians." Now do you know what he is referring to when he refers to infiltrations of -- infiltration of armed groups?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- I'm sure the military will account for certain aspects, but CIVPOL also would have encountered incidents. Indeed, I would think if you look over that period of time, you my find there were murders committed in the UNPAs. I referred to earlier a number of incidents which took place and I dealt -- or the Croatian authorities actually complained of their people being killed, and I was asked to prepare a report on it, and I examined the records available at that time and it may go back to around that period. And I established that in fact the Croatians had actually killed more Serbs and that was noticed -- that was sent back to them. In addition to that, in the same report we also sought an explanation from them in respect of a situation where a Serb was detained in a Croatian prison and that was recorded as death by suicide. When the body was returned to the family, our monitors carried out an inquiry and they also engaged a British medical doctor, if I can recall correctly, to carry out a post-mortem examination on the body, and they established that this man was beaten to death. And that was sent back to them. So you can see the impact of it is that, you know, there was activity and indeed at that particular moment of time, the figures showed that they were the greater aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Infiltration of armed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please stay closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Infiltration of armed groups is one thing and another thing being referred to is infiltration of civilians. Do you understand what Mr. Andreev was referring to when he referred to infiltration of civilians? Why does he draw that distinction, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- again, I think there is evidence of what I would consider as just maverick groups who just went on a rampage. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You mean to say that there were Croatian maverick groups, as you describe them, crossing over the confrontation line from the Croatian side into the UNPAs and committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a report in existence from down south in -- in -- indicating that that is one of the scenarios for the killings, or some of the killings that has been put forward, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it says there that there were clashes between militia and Croatian police. Now, when I see the word "militia," I often caution myself that it may be a reference to "milicija," namely, the Serb police. As far as you know, were there direct clashes between the Serb milicija and the Croatian police? Were they fighting each other in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what do you call, the group of policemen from within the 700 group are you referring to or the special police as I would?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, there's no reference to special police here. I'm not sure precisely what Mr. Andreev may be referring to you, but what I'm asking you is whether there was any direct confrontation between the regular police on the Serb side, and any Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. During my time there, no, I'm not. But I think historically there were incidents of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how did actual infiltration or the threat of infiltration affect the ability of the police, and by police I mean here the 7.000? How did it affect their ability to conduct law enforcement in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, they were faced with a difficult situation. I suppose you could say they were starting on a playing pitch that was never designed for them either. If you take it, in reality they were coming into a field that wasn't what was promised. If they were starting with the Vance Plan, they were going into what should be a demilitarised area, so you can see the difficulties they had. And we understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And they were not permitted under the Vance Plan to carry anything other than side-arms, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were the groups, the maverick groups that you described, based on what you know, did they tend to be heavily armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what they had, but I would suspect that they would be heavily armed. Yes. Certainly would. I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We would tender this document, although it may already be tendered. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It should come in as an associated exhibit with the statement. This is 1253.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 1290, please, which is Defence tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McElligott, this is the further report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolutions 743 and 762. The date is 19 September 1992. If we could please turn to page 4, paragraph 6. "General Nambiar has repeatedly stressed to the authorities in Belgrade and Knin that is UNPROFOR which exercises the protection function notice UNPAs and that the presence of these paramilitary units is contrary to the United Nations Plan and has caused the Croatian army to retain some of its forces at the confrontation line." Now just an aside there, from the context it appears that the paramilitary forces being referred to -- paramilitary units are the special police. And then he goes on: "As a result, clashes continue to occur along the line, fueling intercommunal tension in the UNPAs." Now, first of all, sir, there's a connection being drawn here between the clashes and the intercommunal tension. Does that correspond with what you know was going on at the -- what was fueling intercommunal tension, amongst other causes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see where just one is sparking off the other. And on it goes. That's where you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that here General Nambiar appears to -- is reported as having asserted that it is indeed UNPROFOR which exercises as, it's put here, the protection function in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what he is saying is simply that the special police should not be there, and if they got a foothold in the situation, you may get a different attitude from the other side, and you may get into discussions, into negotiations, and advance somewhat. So that's what he's saying to them. He's saying, "Look, you're breaking the Vance Plan. The other people don't trust you because you're doing. Please let us take responsibility for what we should be taking responsibility and withdraw," and I think that's the message he is trying to convey and trying to get a starting point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Not only withdraw, disarm; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disarm. It's absolute -- absolutely. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that was the consistent message of UNPROFOR, wasn't it, that UNPROFOR will provide the protection, and therefore these units must be disbanded and there must be full demilitarisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're basically saying give us a chance to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This document is tendered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D70, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01321, please. Prosecution tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a joint commission set up to address various issues between the Croat and Serb side under the auspices of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I think it came as part of the pink zone resolution, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you know whether it was restricted to discussion of pink zone issues or was it an across the board forum for discussion of any issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is from reading some minutes is that it was used actually as a forum to broaden out and engage in a rather broad field. I think it became on occasions quite an open agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the chair of the joint commission was Mr. Thornberry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, yes. The UN chaired the meeting. I think Cedric was the -- generally in charge. I think Viktor may have -- Andreev may have also chaired some meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Chairman's report: "The presence of these armed irregular forces was totally unacceptable. He wished also to ask the Serb delegation for a clarification of recent statements attributed to, inter alios, Mr. Goran Hadzic and Mr. Milan Martic, in which they had been reported as saying that their authorities did not accept the basic elements of Resolution 762 and wished to renegotiate the Vance Plan." Now, is this another example of UNPROFOR pressuring for complete demilitarisation of any forces in the UNPAs on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been able to read the document, but ... Could you start where -- enlarge it slightly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If it helps, it's in the binder in the first lot of documents, if you prefer to look at the hard copy. 1321.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the early stage of the folder? Could you lead me to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 2, sir. The first paragraph, under "Chairman's report."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does this again reflect that UNPROFOR at the highest levels is insisting on complete, full, and absolute demilitarisation of the Serb side in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are asking for demilitarisation. That is the Vance Plan coming into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is about a month and a half after Mr. Andreev's report. You remember we looked at that, the second-last document, in which he said there was a danger of a threat of Croatian attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And notably there's no reference in this document to that threat, is there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that paragraph. I haven't read the rest. But again, it reflects the slowness of the situation, the mistrust. At least they're still talking and, you know, that's the way you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But my point is that here we have UNPROFOR asking for full and complete demilitarisation at the very moment when they know, based on their own intelligence, that Croatian forces are as was said in the second-last document mobilising; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I have no doubt they are talking to them as well and trying to calm the situation down and bring them into discussions, negotiations, and adjust the position they're holding. And that's what I said earlier, you're taking one step back -- or forward or maybe taking two steps backward. So all you can say is you still have them talking in some fashion, and they haven't gone into total aggression because that is where it could go, is total head-on, and I think if the UN wasn't there to create that type of engagement, you know, where would you have gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the basis of this demand that full demilitarisation should take place is General Nambiar's assurance, an assurance provided on other occasions I'm sure, that UNPROFOR would protect those areas, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's saying let's go back to the Vance Plan. You said you would give your full commitment to getting engaged in it and so forth and get it into a proper beginning. And he is then saying, "Well, we have a role to play, we will do it." And again you can see that could be a very difficult role, extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, it was one that would probably take years. So we were never going to solve it in a day, or a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the role is to militarily protect the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To protect the protected areas. And I think again the military protect is referred to in -- the role of the military is referred to as the level of engagement is by, you know, more or less basically defending themselves and limited force. And again, once you got to that point, you are looking at negotiating, negotiating, and stabilising. Using -- using your fire-arm should be the last option in your situation. And you know, there's a lot of space for talk in between. The day you go to the gun, you have lost the real purpose of going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go to 03170, please. Defence tab 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, am I right, sir, about two months after this meeting, the joint commission meeting that we've just looked at, on or around the 21st January there was a major Croatian offensive --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- against the area in which Benkovac was located; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, as best you know about that event what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the attack took place from Maslenica bridge and they came forward certainly to Benkovac because I was there that morning, and the town was shelled from what I know. And the population fled from the countryside ahead of it. And many of them ended up at the CIVPOL station in Benkovac. When I was departing that morning on the 22nd, the hotel reception area was full of civilians. The car park area was crowded. There are accounts there of people being injured. There's an account there of a lady starting to give birth to a child. It -- there was -- they were in absolute panic, and our monitors took some -- the -- people injured and casualties to hospital, they dealt with the lady who was giving birth, and these people were in absolute terror. And that was the -- the civilian impact on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Many civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the figures myself, but there were. There were many from what I know, yeah. I don't have the actual figures here. I'm unfamiliar with them. But there were casualties, human casualties, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Artillery --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I think when -- our monitors who were held hostage went to the hospital and with -- with some patients, and they saw several people at the hospital injured and very seriously injured. So they saw first-hand the fallout.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Artillery shelling of urban areas, including Benkovac --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- believe it or not, I slept through the whole thing and I had to be called in the morning. But I -- I -- I was aware of it when I got up. Let's put it that way. I slept soundly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'd like, if I may, to ... turn to page 2 of this document. And this is, again, General Nambiar. And he's writing to Mr. Goulding. At paragraph 5, down at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think that that document is the right one. In fact, you don't have this one in your binder, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But we could perhaps dispense with the B/C/S on the screen and just zoom in on the English. "The credibility of the various parties to the conflict in this region has always been debatable, but what we have been subjected to over the last few days has made it impossible to place any value on any assurances that are given, no matter what the level. A senior colleague has used the term surreal too describe conduct which none of us, in our diverse years and fields of experience has previously encountered at high levels of government. This factor will have a serious effect on future discussions and negotiations." Now I suggest that in paragraphs 4 and 5 he is talking about the Croatian side, and then here we have at paragraph 6 his analysis of the Serb side: "On the Serb side, as I mentioned in one of my earlier cables, we are seen as traitors and betrayers. This is mainly because we had relied on Croatian assurances of willingness to sit and talk and had persuaded many of our Serb interlocutors of that faith. While the vehemence of their denunciation is beginning to abate as some see what the real situation was, I cannot see them placing their weaponry back into storage areas in the near future." Did you understand at this time that in fact it turned out that UNPROFOR felt completely betrayed by the Croatian assurances that they would not attack the UNPAs and the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLET
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just in relation to which side is being referred to in which paragraph. I see in paragraph 4 they are referring to the political parties in Croatia, but then at paragraph 5 the opening line says: "The credibility of the various parties to the conflict in this region..." And my learned friend has suggested that both these paragraphs refer to the Croatian side but that didn't seem to reflect what had been read onto the record in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's my interpretation. My learned friend is more than welcome to ask further questions on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it clearly sets out General Nambiar's position at that time, the difficulties he had. It -- there's no doubt. You can see the difficulties of the mission. They are truly reflected there, and the level of negotiation and confidence-building that would have to take place before you could advance anywhere. You know, it's -- I think it focuses precisely how the stalemate was there and he almost -- there's a level of frustration on his part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you were present there at the time. And presumably you were in communication with your colleagues in UNPROFOR. Did you hear whether UNPROFOR took any steps to prevent this attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR is -- their role at that point was negotiate, negotiate. And you go back to the Vance Plan for your beginning, and you have got to say to yourself: "No, this is where we are beginning with defence, and the pitch is not where we should have it." Do they become the aggressors at that point? And I don't think -- I certainly wouldn't envisage it as being the way to go about it. And all you can do is negotiate and get people talking and try and withdraw in -- in a -- in a sensible way, to put it mildly, and you're looking at those with the authority and the responsibility at the highest level of government there to be talked and the difficulties UN is encountering with them. And that is the type of change that they were pursuing, and you can see the difficulty of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We've reached that time. And also, Mr. Gosnell, I am still looking at what you said about paragraph -- paragraphs 4 and 5 of this document. If it is -- I don't have it on the screen. But if as Mr. Gillett said paragraph 5 says, "The credibility of the various parties to the conflict in this region," what you call your interpretation would rather be a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I should respond to your question in the absence of the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's the time for our first break. We will be back in 30 minutes. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have paragraph 5 on the screen, please. Oh, we have it. The -- we have it here, yes. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I believe it's beyond dispute that paragraph 5 is referring to the Croatian side, notwithstanding that preamble in the first sentence where he says "the credibility of all parties." And the reason I say that is because you see the discussion in paragraph 4 which is all about the position on the Croatian side, including a speech by -- or an interview given by president Tudjman to "Der Spiegel." And then if you look at the second and third sentences of that paragraph, and in fact even the first sentence itself, there's only one side whose assurances could be being referred to. It's definitely not the Serb side. There are no Serb assurances under discussion. It's the Croatian assurances that are in discussion. And in that context, I say that it's quite clear that this is referring to the Croatian side. There's nothing in -- in the context that would suggest that this is in any way referring to assurances that have been given by the Serbs or that anything that they had done would have been described as surreal. That can only be the Croatian side. And the discussion of what the Serbs are doing is in paragraph 6 and beyond because that goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I -- I may have jumped up precipitously, and I do see that possible interpretation. I also think there is a possible interpretation that paragraph 4 refers to the Croatian side, paragraph 5 is more of a general paragraph, and paragraph 6 is referring to the Serb side. But I may have jumped up too early on this point. It just was the first sentence that put me off at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now just before the break, Mr. McElligott, you said that UNPROFOR's role at that point was negotiate, negotiate. But, in fact, UNPROFOR's role was broader under the Vance Plan, wasn't it? Its role was to protect the protected areas from fear of armed attack.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was its mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the Maslenica or Benkovac attack, as I think you refer to it, that was a major failure for the UNPROFOR mission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept it in that term. I think that the UNPROFOR mission was never one of going to war with another nation.
