utterances.text: I saw that as an extreme -- as a very serious risk, risk to our people, and I raised the matter with Cedric Thornberry to take it up with the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did someone on the Serb side tell you that it was there -- the purpose of them being held there was to serve as human shields?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police monitor who was given the job of taking them hostage, and I said to him -- I said before he was a very honourable man. He told them that they were going to be taken hostage and -- so that was the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, being taken hostage -- and I don't think I'm splitting hairs here. But being taken hostage or detained or being restricted from free movement is one thing. Being used as a human shield is quite another. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they were being used for. They were put onto the top floor, or the third floor, and that was what they were for. And we had other intelligence to say that would happen in respect of other installations, if they came under attack. It didn't stand alone on this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's come back to my question. Did someone on the Serb side tell you that they were being used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had it from other sources that our monitors and other civilian staff in UNPROFOR would be taken hostage to act as human shields. And that's the simple call on it. If you were put into an installation and put in there strategically so that the installation would not be attacked. That's the simple version. I wouldn't call it anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So this -- how far in advance of this event taking place were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is stated on the report made by Mitchell. I think it's two days in advance but -- I think it's 17th, 16th. It's actually specifically referred to, when he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was he told that they would be not permitted to leave Benkovac as a means of deterring an incursion by Croatian forces? Or was he told - and maybe you don't know this - was he told that they were going to be used specifically as human shields at a military location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no doubt in any of our minds that if the situation arose, we were to be used as human shields. No doubt. And we were very conscious of that risk for our people in the field. I wouldn't call it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you use the term "human shield," do you understand it to have meant and now do you understand it to mean that you would be held at a military location, a military -- a place that could be militarily targeted to provide protection for that location and facility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the information we had went beyond that. They were going to even use it for facilities such as electrical stations or whatever. So, again, what you're doing is you're putting something in front of the opposition to say do you want to go down that road take on the international community. You had 21 monitors there from, I would say, perhaps ten nations. You can see the implications of that. So it was a very strategic move and it's placing lives at serious risk. And we mentioned earlier that there were always people, mavericks, who will do their own thing, so no matter what control you have of your sources -- of your resources, there can be an individual who will just blow the place away. So it was a real, real risk to our people. And I'll tell you something, it left its mark on many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say there are mavericks who might do anything, are you suggesting that the individuals who directed the detention of these UNCIVPOL monitors, were they acting on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By those who were planning the strategies to resist the attack and, indeed, any attack from Croatian sources. As I mentioned, the information was available and it also included installations. So it wasn't just it happened on the day for this situation. It was a planned situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, who was involved exactly; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the day, I would think you could go back up to the Kenyan authorities. It was a strategic plan. You have to go back to a serious level of the management.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Spanovic in on it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was in -- you look at a strategic op -- a strike like that, it has to be at a serious level because they are literally challenging the international community. They're saying to you: We're taking your people and we are going to use you. They're drawing other nations into the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it true that at one point during the hostage taking some of the UN observers were escorted outside of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they at gunpoint when they drove to the hospital in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were. And indeed I remember, if I recall correctly, they asked to go down to the local police station, that's the UNPROFOR office, and were refused permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How far is the hotel in Benkovac from the hospital in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be 50 miles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The UN observers were held at gunpoint while being driven 50 miles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held at gunpoint, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while, as you suggest, they were being held at gunpoint during this 50-mile journey, did you hear that at one point, notwithstanding that they were under milicija escort, you say at gunpoint, notwithstanding that they were under milicija escort, that they were run off the road by an angry Serb soldier. Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an incident, yes, and they were shot at. And I would say indeed their own assessment was despite the fact -- they felt they would have been killed only for the presence of the other people, and basically the point I'm making on it, and they made, was even despite the peer pressure of their own people, these guys reacted and fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And wasn't there another incident, a separate incident right in front of the hotel when another angry soldier saw the UN Land Cruiser and used an automatic rifle and fired almost 40 bullets into the car? Didn't that occur too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And again it highlights, if our monitors were free, would they stay there? Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to conclusions in a moment. Isn't it the case that there were two French soldiers who were killed --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- by a mortar shell and essentially they were killed on impact, instantly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the military operation was ongoing for at least seven days, possibly more?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on for a period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And their release happened to coincide with the end of the military offensive, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The release -- no, the release commenced with my going down there. My going down there wasn't designed on what was happening in the greater picture. I just came to a point where nothing was happening to get them out and I took the initiative to go on that particular day. That wasn't written by other agendas, let's put it that way, other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That -- that wasn't my question. The question was: Their release coincided with the end of the military operation, did it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think we mentioned earlier that it went down to Benkovac -- or into -- approached the dam up to the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree that to an outside observer, there was a very credible basis to think that unarmed, and you were unarmed, that unarmed UN officials might be under threat or danger either from the fighting or from elements amongst the Serb forces who were out of control, angry, in particular at the UN at this point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always felt that being unarmed was perhaps the best weapon we had, for the use of a word, in the sense that we were not going to cause danger to anybody. And we always believed that was the best approach to take and to ensure our safety. And that's the way it was. And you can see that in this situation, we were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me be clear about what I'm asking you. I'm not suggesting necessarily that everyone who was involved in this incident was animated by a genuine desire to protect the observers. What I'm suggesting to you is, from an outside perspective, wouldn't a reasonable observer be able to say, Well, maybe there was legitimate reason to not permit the UN observers to drive around under these circumstances, for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You go back and you ask the observers who were involved what the facts are and they are quite clear that they were hostages, and there is no other call on that. And they are quite clear on that. And I think there's nowhere else to go with it, in my view. It's quite honest, saying that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You don't know what Mr. Hadzic may have been told before he gave the press conference that you were shown by the Prosecution during your testimony, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not privy to his briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you some questions about returns of internally displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could have, please, 01212. That's Defence tab 23. This is the Secretary-General's report of the 27th of July, 1992. If we could go to page 6, which is paragraph 18: "The Force Commander estimates that the conditions do not yet exist for a large-scale voluntary return programme into the UNPAs."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that view widely shared amongst UNPROFOR officials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1-0 -- excuse me, 01253. Prosecution tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a status report and we've looked at this before. I'm not going to discuss it again. But the date is the 7th of September, 1992. If we could turn to page 3, please. "Return of displaced Croats." And then we're looking for a sentence that begins: "But the latest escalation of events in Sector South, Croatian rights violations included, indicated that it might be unrealistic to carry out any return in the forthcoming future. It is necessary to carefully consider the dangers of jeopardizing the entire process of return in phase 3. But when started, even in limited manner, Croatians will expand it elsewhere, and uncontrolled mass-scale return with possible escalation into war." Can you help us understand why -- if you can, can you help us understand why the author is making that comment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a couple of comments there. First of all, it is about coming in in small numbers and scaling it in. I think in reality there was no scope to go down that road. And I think what's being indicated then is even if you do, you will be taken advantage of. And the other side will push on to go beyond the boundaries of what your plan may have been in bringing in a minimal group and just trying to take one step forward and that it would be exploited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01273, please. Again this is a document that we've looked at. It's Defence tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is General Nambiar reporting to Goulding on the 22nd of September, 1992. And that date is significant, September 1992, because wasn't there much discussion about a planned mass return of refugees at the end of the month?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then -- and in this first paragraph, we've looked at it before, General Nambiar says: "Perhaps you might also bring home to him," him being Tudjman, "the disastrous consequences which could ensure if the proposed mass march of refugees into Sector East were to take place on 30 September." Was that the view of UNPROFOR that that march was not a good idea?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR opposed it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether UNPROFOR took any steps to prevent it from taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the steps UNPROFOR would be taking would be ones of negotiation to downscale the likelihood of it happening. Now what they actually did, I do not know. But I would see that as being the road they would go. And, again, with respect to negotiating yourself out of a serious conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01290, please, which is Defence tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Again, further report of the Secretary-General dated the 29th of September, 1992. Am I right in recalling that this is the day before the scheduled mass march that we've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the actually date of it now, on -- off the top of my head but it's somewhere at the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to page 9 in e-court. Paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "However, constant agitation by the media and certain political authorities for immediate return is building up dangerous pressures, with unilaterally proclaimed timetables for return and advertised mass marches to the sectors. UNPROFOR has told the authorities that such exploitation of the deep and very understandable desire of people to return to their homes is irresponsible. Ill-timed and uncoordinated returns could lead to a further disaster."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's real, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Croatia playing -- let me put it a bit more neutrally. Was Croatia using the issue of the return of internally displaced persons as a wedge to accomplish goals in the war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in my view that this issue was being driven to further other agendas, yes. These civilian people were just being used. And I think if we look at some of the reports from the other side, the Serbian side, you will see that there was an increasing of a military response on that side of the house. I think there are mention of reports where we had people armed with AK-47s and going to Batina bridge, and if you have a mass march of innocent civilians walking into that situation, what is the outcome? It's pushing the board out a long way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gillett, re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I'll try and go through this -- a couple of points quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So, Mr. McElligott, again I'll ask you to speak slowly and clearly. Thank you? If we go back, at transcript page 47 you were asked about the regular police and ability to control the special police. You said: "From the police side there were difficulties. They had confided in us on occasion that the special police were out of their control." Can I just clarify who you mean by "they" when you say "they had confided"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the -- the normal police had confided on us, to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know any individuals who were confiding that information or is it a more general response?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met one or two myself who did tell me, that they had a problem. It has emerged in some of the reports as well or it was declared. There were men there who wanted to police and there is no doubt their hands were tied. They couldn't do their job and they did it as best they could at local level, and that's where their goodwill and their commitment came into -- at just local level they were able to do the thing in their own corner as best they could. And there were times when they had to back away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McElligott, I think the identity of the "they" is clear enough. Another clarification, at transcript page 66 you were asked about essentially the possibility of opportunist crime being an explanation for some of these crimes referred to in report 5404. And you said that: "There is always an element in any context of this type of crime." And then you said that: "Then you have another situation, what is left behind, that has to be addressed as well." What did you mean by that second sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the people who were committing crime and who were dressed in uniform. I think, you know, if you are a police force and you receive a complaint from a victim that the person engaging it has a police uniform or a police identity, you would take a very, very serious view of it, first of all, to establish your own credibility as a police force and, secondly, to reassure the community of the facts of the situation. And if you found it to be some policemen involved, that you would take very effective measures to make sure your professional standards are maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to crimes by police members, you were asked whether Hadzic was ever contacted in relation to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get document 65 ter 5312 on the monitor, please. And as this is coming up, you'll see it's a similar protest, it's a pair of protest letters similar to ones that have been admitted through this witness. I'm interested in the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, on the second page, this is a letter from Nambiar, Force Commander. It says: "I write this letter to express my deep concern at the deliberate shooting of one of our Military Observers on 21 December 1992 in the Bapska area in Sector East." Now would you consider that a criminal matter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And why would that be sent to Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is also --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, the witness has commented on a number of protest letters sent to Mr. Hadzic concerning shelling and other topics, and he was asked about this in cross-examination, whether letters would be sent to Mr. Hadzic, so I'm verifying whether he does have an opinion based on his experience with UNCIVPOL as to why this letter would have been sent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would also be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you could answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would also be a very serious breach of the Vance Plan agreement. Our monitors were entitled to free movement and this would certainly inhibit your movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph it also refers to restrictions of movement in place. I know this is covered in your statement in quite a lot of detail, so I won't ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I would ask to admit this document, 5312, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In relation to Benkovac, you were asked about the reason for which the UNCIVPOL monitors who were taken hostage were accompanied by armed militia. Now, your forces, as you've said, were unarmed, correct, and they were always unarmed while they were in the region, and did they face dangers at other times other than at the Benkovac incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed they did. They were confronted on various ways along the period of their service. They were held at gunpoint on prior occasions. There's -- I recall a specific incident where they were held at gunpoint and indeed the interpreter stepped in between them and literally -- I did declare that they would have to take her out if they wanted to take the monitors out and she eventually settled the situation down and got them back out of the situation safe. And they had been robbed at gunpoint. There was a series of serious crimes committed against our monitors at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, that's referred to in the statement. And in instances other than Benkovac, were your monitors provided armed guards as has been suggested by my learned friend for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- we have never been provided with armed guards but we have gone on joint patrols with the military, I think KenBat is specifically mentioned to -- in the Sector South, and again, that the basic idea behind that was to spread our resources and our capacity to engage in a lot of patrols by having, perhaps, one policeman in a car and accompanied by a soldier or two soldiers. Now I do not know if they carried weapons, but in general principle, as police officers we would generally not allow a situation where you're going to have somebody with arms engaging with or be with -- or be accompanying somebody who doesn't be armed. We go for the neutral situation because if the gun is there, the opposition are likely to engage with us, or readily, so we don't want to expose the unarmed person. And the philosophy is to go back to unarmed for safety of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Final question. In relation to the issue of the attempted mass return in late 1992, you've been asked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if I could call document 65 ter 1277, this is from the Defence list, on the monitor. And if we could go to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you were asked several questions about this document during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's 1277. Thank you. And if we could zoom in near the bottom, there is ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: There is a bullet point that reads: "The recent violations of human rights in the pink zone, mainly destruction of houses already burned, of churches, are messages to warn against any return of DPs," which I take it to mean displaced persons. Did that have an impact on the conditions for the return of people to these areas in which you operated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Of course, yes. Again it was creating the unstable environment. Taking down the churches and the houses was, as I've said earlier, literally breaking down the sense of community. Church was a place where people went where there was very often social engagement by old folk who may not meet from one end of the week to the other, so there was -- just apart from a religious element, there was a community side to it as well. So it was destabilising the whole community approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We'd tender 1277 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will escort you out of the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the meanwhile, it has been confirmed that we can sit this afternoon for an extra session starting at 3.00, 3.00 to 4.30, and I thank everyone who is facilitating this to enable us to finish this week's witness. If there's nothing else, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just one comment that may assist with scheduling. I may well have no more than five minutes of cross-examination. I don't know whether that might accelerate our plans or not. I just thought I would say that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think we could -- we could take the witness immediately and -- and -- and finish the witness within this session. I don't think that's a realistic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President we've confirmed that the Defence -- sorry the Prosecution direct examination is still to be previewed to be at 30 minutes or so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- so we can't finish by 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's stick to the plan, and we'll see each other at 3.00, and probably we will be out before 4.30. Thank you very much. Court adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I, for the record, indicate that the Hadzic Defence is joined at this time by legal intern Jolana Makraiova. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I should say now for the Prosecution, we have with us in the courtroom, Ms. Sarah Clanton and legal intern, Marija Bukovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. I will ask you in a few minutes to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses comment themselves to tell the truth, and I have to point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could I ask you to stand for a moment and make the solemn declaration the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Clanton, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Your Honour, I note that I don't believe we introduced the witness. Would you like for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're right. I forgot to ask her name and date of birth. Could you give us -- tell us, Ms. Witness, Madam Witness, what your name and date of birth is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sarlota Foro. I was born on the 4th of January, 1963, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, do you recall that you testified here in The Hague in November 2005 in the case of Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And since you arrived here in The Hague this week, have you had an opportunity to listen to the audio recording of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I got an audio recording and I re-listened to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is there anything in your testimony that you listened to this week that you no longer believe to be correct?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There's only one detail regarding the identification of a person from a picture that was shown to me during that trial. The picture doesn't show the whole person, just the hands, or arms, so obviously by mistake, I misidentified the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And to make the record clear, Ms. Foro, who was the person that you misidentified based on the hands?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That's Major Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, with the exception of the change to your evidence that you just discussed with us, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked when you testified before, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: As for the rest of the statement, I stand by it fully, except for that one detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I stated everything correctly. And my testimony was truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would seek to tender Prosecution 65 ter Exhibits 04638.1 and 04638.2, which are at tab 14. We would also seek to tender the associated exhibits with the exception of associated exhibits 02601 and 02990, these are at tabs 2 and number 12. And the reason that we would not seek to tender these is that these are the exhibits that relate to the correction that the witness has just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2186 and P2187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now for the first question I want to ask you has to do with your testimony about the events in Vukovar in the Autumn 1991. You said that the people in Vukovar were living in shelters or cellars because of the bombing that was happening, and this is at transcript page 2399 for the record. You further testified that the destruction in Vukovar had reached a point that because the roofs and the walls were missing, projectiles were falling down the level of the shelters and there were civilian casualties that resulted. And this is transcript page 2409. Can you describe for the Chamber a particular instance in which this happened.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: If you give me the right to describe the events that were happening already in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If there was a particular instance that occurred at that time, yes, please, do continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: In 1991, at that time, at the time that you referred to, and that was already the month of November when the devastation of the city had reached such a degree that even in shelters people were not safe anymore, an incident happened involving our family friend, who got killed with his entire family in a shelter in the centre of the town. He got killed, his wife, his mother, and his very small child. Another young man was killed on occasion. What happened was that a projectile flew in through the window of the shelter and exploded. Those are the civilian casualties that I spoke about last time, and such things were happening already in November 1991. People were getting killed in large numbers even in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Foro, you've just told us that there was a very small child that was killed as a result of this projectile exploding in a shelter. Can you tell us, what did you hear later on about this small child?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Specifically it was the family Aleksandar, the name of the child was Matija Aleksandar. The parent's names were Vlasta and Emil. The Aleksandars were our family friends because the husband worked with my -- with my husband. The next thing I heard of it, I next thing I saw, was when I came to Sremska Mitrovica where I was for questioning and on the desk of the colonel who was conducting the questioning, I saw a Belgrade newspaper with the photo of the little child that was killed on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what were you asked about the photo of this child on the front page of the Belgrade newspaper?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: They didn't ask me anything. They just maintained that the child was a Serb child who had its throat killed by the Croats; one among 40 Serb children who were killed by Croats. That was a very notorious scandal at the time and it was in all the media, all over the media. The colonel who was conducting the interrogation put that to me, and I said that I have completely different information about the case, and I can share it with him, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when you offered to share this information to him, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: He asked me to explain. And I explained it in the same way as I did to the Court today. I said the name of the child, who the parents were, under what circumstances the child was killed, and I also made a written statement about it in longhand, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what did you find out thereafter about this story about the 40 children being -- being killed.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Later on, I found out that some sort of a scandal, a outcry had broken out in Serbia in that connection because all the allegations printed in the press right after the fall of Vukovar were later refuted by the same journalist who made the initial report, or perhaps his editorial team. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You previously testified that due to the destruction and the shortage of ammunition and food that it became clear to the -- the people, including yourself, in Vukovar, that could you no longer remain in the city. This is at transcript page 2409. You said that when the people of Vukovar realised that Vukovar would be occupied that they decided to begin surrender negotiation with the JNA and, for the record, is this at page 2410 and 2411. The question I want to ask you now is: What concerns did the Croats in Mitnica have about an occupation by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Considering that I mentioned several times in my statement that the war in Vukovar was waged by the local residents. People who had their families there, who lived there, and some of them were members of the ZNG, the Home Guards Corps. Some were members of the defence effort, they just guarded their own homes, but most of them were members of the ZNG who later surrendered at Mitnica and their families lived precisely in that part of the city in that neighbourhood. What worried them and all the other people the most at that time was what was going to happen with the civilians, women and children, who had lived in basements those three months. At the command of the ZNG, they debated how to approach it and on what conditions to talk to the JNA about the surrender of that part of the town. The conditions that I mean is that all civilians be able to go to the unoccupied part of Croatia, the part of Croatia that was not a war zone; and the second was that the members of the ZNG would surrender and lay down their arms on the condition that they be treated as prisoners of war, and that they be registered or filmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, a moment -- excuse me, if I can stop you there, I'm going to go back to something you just said. You said that the members of the ZNG or the Home Guard Corps and some were member of the defence effort who guarded their own homes, that these were people -- were you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Now I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask my question again. A moment ago, you said that the people who were members of the ZNG, or the Home Guard Corps, were involved in civilian protection, defence of their homes, you said that they were the people from your area and that they were worried about what was going to happen to the civilians. And I want to ask you to tell us why they were worried about what would happen to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, the circumstances were as follows: The citizens of Vukovar had been shelled for the previous three months from all the heavy weaponry of the JNA as the only armed force that had that kind of weaponry in the former Yugoslavia. The city was devastated and the civilians were in basements. A large number of civilians had been killed by that time. What concerned us all, civilians and members of the ZNG alike, was why would the Yugoslav People's Army which had tried to kill all of us civilians and destroy the entire city, why would they suddenly change their behaviour once they occupy the city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could clarify with the witness what the witness meant when saying that "the war in Vukovar" -- "in Vukovar was waged by the local residents." It's at -- it's at page 109, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, are you able to respond to the Presiding Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I don't know which passage is meant, which part of my evidence? If you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall I read it to the witness, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If you could. I'm sorry, mine is frozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, you -- you -- you answered to Ms. Clanton the following in the English record, that is. I quote: "Considering that I mentioned several times in my statement that the war in Vukovar was waged by the local residents." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What was it -- what was it that you said? Do you remember? There's probably a problem with the translation. So do you remember what you -- what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just explained that members of the Home Guards Corps, the ZNG, the Croatian army that we are discussing, where indeed the Croatian army and they were indeed armed, but in all parts of Vukovar they had been recruited from the local population, the population of that area. So in the course of the evacuation of the city and the surrendering of the troops at Mitnica, all these people were people who normally lived at Mitnica with their families and were part of the Croatian army. I don't know if I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, a moment ago we were talking about the situation in Vukovar concerning the JNA. I want to ask you now, what, if anything, did you know about the activities of the JNA in the towns and villages outside Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: We knew that already in October some places were occupied and evacuated, some places between Vukovar and Serbia - that is to say, Ilok, Sarengrad and Sotin - and it was known that these places had been occupied and the population evacuated or displaced. Of course we listened to the radio as well, up to a certain point we were able to watch television, and we learned some things from both the Croat and the Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how did this information about what had happened to the populations in Ilok, Sarengrad and Sotin, how did this information affect you?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Of course, the people who were hearing what was going on around them, not far away from them, were afraid. And they were thinking what our own fate might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the assistance of the Case Manager, please, to bring up 65 ter 04780.9.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up I want to ask you, Ms. Foro, what were the names of the Croat negotiators?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were three of them: Zdravko Komsic, Matija Mandic and Filip Karaula. They were practically the command of the Home Guard Corps for that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: For the record, this is a video-clip from the video ERN V000-686, and the clip is time code 8 minutes and 45 seconds to 9 minutes and 2 seconds. And, thank you, I'm reminded there is no need for a transcript here. We are only going to look at the images, and I would like to ask for the video to be played but paused at 8 minutes and 47 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Foro, who are the persons who are walking in the line behind the soldier?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Behind the armed soldier is Filip Karaula, followed by Matija Mandic and Zdravko Kondic [as interpreted]. They were together.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, can you repeat the last name of the third person, Zdravko, and I don't think we got the last name.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Zdravko Komsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask for this video to be played to the 9-minute mark, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Foro, who is on the far left side of the shot?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Filip Karaula, one of the negotiators on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, the person next to him, the one who is wearing sun-glasses, do you know what this person was doing at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, since you arrived in The Hague were you able to watch a longer version of this video?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I've seen the entire video-clip, which is perhaps an hour long, maybe a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And from viewing this video-clip, are you able to indicate what the role or the position was of the person wearing the sun-glasses?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: He's obviously the interpreter for the representative of the ICRC who was also there. At the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would want to tender this clip, 65 ter 04780.9, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Foro, you testified in the Mrksic case that after these negotiations took place, that the negotiators went back to Mitnica and they said that you would be going to a collection point which is near a veterinary clinic in approximately one hour in order to prepare for departure and this is at transcript page 2417.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the Case Manager's assistance, please, to pull up video with 65 ter number 4780.11. And this is a clip of the same video from the same -- with the same ERN and the time code is from 43 minutes, 42 seconds to 47 minutes and 52 seconds. And I would like for the Case Manager to play it and please pause at 43 minutes and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, from the view on the screen in front of you, can you tell the Court where the collection point was located?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was not a collection centre. It was a place that everybody knew, everybody knew where it was. That is the veterinary clinic at Mitnica. The road widen there a bit and that's the place where they told us it would be best for us to come and form a column, a convoy, to exit Vukovar. This place is just before this road sign on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, in what direction are the people that we see between the tanks, in what direction are they walking?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: In the direction of the new cemetery at Mitnica. Towards the exit from Vukovar. You can see the sign, Vukovar, in blue, and from there, in that direction, you walk towards the new cemetery, towards Sotin and Vucilevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now if I can ask the Case Manager to please skip forward to 46 minutes and 52 seconds. And if we could play here until 46 minutes and 58 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, do you recognise this woman?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That is a neighbour who lives in the same street where my husband used to live with his parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And where were you at the time that this footage was being taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was already -- also walking in that column.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would seek to tender 65 ter 04780.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I just ask how -- how long the clip is that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The clip is 4 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what is on the other 4 minutes of the video or whether the witness has commented on any of it. I would prefer to only have the portions that the witness has been shown and commented upon admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I am skipping to this point for the sake of time. If I could ask for Your Honours to give us an additional ten minutes on the direct then I would be happy to play the 4-minute clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes to play the 4-minute clip, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In addition to the time that I would -- 30 minutes I would request to have a bit more time so that we could build in the time to play the 4-minute clip, please. If this is a concern to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, you'll have five minutes extra.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Laugel, could we go back to, I believe we stopped at 43:42, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Get on the tank. Get on the tank. Go on, get on the tank. "We need to get down to the Red Cross. Just get down to the Red Cross. Let's go down to the Red Cross, eh? "Sorry -- down. Down. "Where is the next ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Foro, I want to ask you is everything we've seen in this video-clip just now, is this consistent with what you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Everything on the video is consistent with what happened. There's nothing that happened in a different place. Everything that we see in the video did happen there. I just want to say that it's just a small fraction of what happened during that day. This video does not show us anything like a full picture of what transpired that day. I have seen the whole video. I mean, the whole video doesn't show what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, would you agree that this video-clip that you've just seen now is an accurate depiction of part of what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: We would like to tender this video-clip at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar how much time I have left, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How much do you need, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: About five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's okay. Sorry. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, the last topic that I want to talk to you about today, to ask you about, is your experience at Sremska Mitrovica. Now, you've given evidence about how you arrived at Sremska Mitrovica. And I want to ask you where were you and the other women taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: We were taken to the prison at Sremska Mitrovica, and we were locked up in a large room inside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in this large room, were there any persons in the room who did not come with you on the bus that you were on from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Mostly those were women who had come from Ovcara and Dr. Bosanac was brought two days later, I think, along with two other young women, who, as far as I know, were not from Mitnica. They, too, were brought a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what happened to these two women who were not from Mitnica who came a couple of days later?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: If I remember well, one of them was injured by shrapnel; a smaller injury. They were with us very briefly, and then they were taken away from our room.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What did you find out what happened after they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I found out they had been taken to a different part of the prison where isolation cells were, and there they were interrogated and abused.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Since you arrived in The Hague, have you had an opportunity to see a list of names containing -- lists of names with people from Sremska Mitrovica on it?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I did see a list of names. And that list names of names is very familiar because it originates from the office where I worked after I came to Zagreb following the events we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 02406.2 brought up. This at tab 27. And this is a document that was circulated by e-mail yesterday. The Defence indicated that they don't have any objection for this document to be added to the 65 ter list, so we would request that it be added and made available to the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Request granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, do you recognise the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I do. I reviewed that list, and I signed the first and the last page of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could please turn to page 4 of the list. This is ERN ending in 8716. Now, Ms. Foro, we see that the number 136 is circled and there's a letter A next to the name Bosanac, Vesna. What does this marking mean?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That means that Dr. Bosanac, Vesna Bosanac, was with me in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now above this row in line number 135, we see that -- that number is also circled and that there's a letter B next to the name Bosanac, Lavoslav. Can you tell us why there's a B next to this name?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Because, to the best of my knowledge, Lavoslav Bosanac was also locked up in the Sremska Mitrovica prison. He is the husband of Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know who Lavoslav Bosanac was before you saw his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, can you confirm that the marking of the letter A throughout is the same for the other markings as it is for Dr. Bosanac, that is, that you've indicated with a letter A if it was somebody who was in your room?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: All the persons that I recognised from this list as having been in the prison at Sremska Mitrovica with me, I marked with an A.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that throughout you marked with a B, as you did for line 135, the persons that you knew?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That's correct. All the people that I knew personally, I knew who they were, I marked with a B.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would seek to tender 02406.2 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Foro, the last thing I want to ask you about is you testified in the Mrksic case that your husband was also held at Sremska Mitrovica. And this is at transcript page 2435. What information did your husband share with you about the conditions for the men who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: According to what he told me, I understood their circumstances had been much worse than ours, and they were regularly mistreated and abused. After being beaten up in Sremska Mitrovica, he came home, missing a tooth, and generally they mistreated them. The men had worse conditions than the women, and their treatment was much worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: During the time that your husband was at Sremska Mitrovica, did he ever tell you about why he was being held there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Nobody talked to them about such things. Nobody gave them any reasons why they were there, just as they did not tell us anything, and we had no opportunity to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Foro. My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings, and I just have a few questions for you. If I'm not clear at all, please feel free to ask me to rephrase, and I'll do my best. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you watch Croatian television in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: 1992? Yes. Yes, I was in Zagreb and I watched Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a programme named "Latinica"?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I just have to say that I didn't watch television too much because I worked in an office that was busy 24 hours a day. We prepared material and other things for exchanges of prisoners and we had little time for TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it a nightly newscast, or a weekly news programme? What exactly was this programme, "Latinica"?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: "Latinica"? I think it was on in the evening. I didn't follow it. I know there was such a programme, but I did not follow it really, with any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, you took shelter during the siege of Vukovar in the cellars of a utility company called Komunalno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I worked at the utility company. Since it was a strategic company for the city under those circumstances, our manager told us, employees, to set up a group if we wished that would be on stand by in that shelter, on stand by, meaning our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many of you were there who took shelter in the basement?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were perhaps ten of us from the utility company, 10 to 15 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then at some point were you joined there by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At one point, when the attacks at Vukovar became more intensive, the command of the ZNG joined us because it was a large cellar, formerly a wine cellar, dug deep into the ground, divided into several rooms, so the command of the Home Guard Corps joined us in that basement, but, of course, they were in a different part of the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did they have some radio equipment with them?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. They had a radio, radio communications. We had a TV set and we had radios where we were able to hear the programmes of Croatian Radio Vukovar, and, of course, we were interested in the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Foro.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything in re-direct, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Foro, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague. You're now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.56 p.m.,
